common_denominators.title: Finding common denominators
common_denominators.big_idea: You can only add or subtract fractions when the pieces are the same size. A common denominator makes the pieces the same size.
steps: Look at the two denominators. If they're different, the pieces are different sizes.
Find a number that both denominators divide into. The smallest one is the lowest common denominator (LCD).
Rewrite each fraction over the LCD. Whatever you multiply the bottom by, multiply the top by the same number.
Now the pieces are the same size, so add or subtract only the numerators. Keep the denominator.
Simplify the answer if you can.
common_denominators.sense_check: Quick check: 1/2 + 1/3 must be more than 1/2, because you're adding something to 1/2. 2/5 is less than 1/2, so 2/5 can't be right.

equivalent_fractions.title: Equivalent fractions
equivalent_fractions.big_idea: Equivalent fractions are the same amount written differently. You make one by multiplying (or dividing) the top and bottom by the same number.
steps: Ask: what do I multiply the old denominator by to get the new one?
Multiply the numerator by that same number.
Check: the fraction should still describe the same amount. Multiplying top and bottom by the same number is like multiplying by 1.
Adding the same number to top and bottom does NOT keep the amount the same.
equivalent_fractions.sense_check: Quick check: 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. Each time the pieces get smaller, you need more of them.

simplifying_fractions.title: Simplifying fractions
simplifying_fractions.big_idea: A fraction is in simplest form when the top and bottom have no common factor except 1.
steps: List the factors of the numerator and the denominator.
Find the greatest common factor (GCF).
Divide the top and the bottom by the GCF.
Check that no number other than 1 divides both.
simplifying_fractions.sense_check: Quick check: 6/8 and 3/4 are the same amount, but 3/4 is simpler because 3 and 4 share no factor.

comparing_fractions.title: Comparing fractions
comparing_fractions.big_idea: A bigger denominator means the whole is cut into more pieces, so each piece is smaller.
steps: If the numerators are the same, the fraction with the smaller denominator is larger.
If the denominators are the same, the fraction with the larger numerator is larger.
Otherwise, rewrite both over a common denominator and compare the numerators.
Sense-check with benchmarks like 1/2: is each fraction more or less than half?
comparing_fractions.sense_check: Quick check: would you rather have 1/3 of a pizza or 1/8? Eight slices are smaller than three slices.

multiply_fractions.title: Multiplying fractions
multiply_fractions.big_idea: Multiplying fractions means taking a part of a part. Multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms.
steps: You do NOT need a common denominator to multiply.
Multiply numerator × numerator.
Multiply denominator × denominator.
Simplify the result.
multiply_fractions.sense_check: Quick check: half of a half is a quarter, so 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Multiplying two fractions less than 1 gives a smaller answer.
